definition: An ease-out's SPEED itself carries a physical claim: a normal, gradual ease-out reads as energy dissipating (the moving thing is slowing down because it's losing energy), while a deliberately fast/snappy ease-out on the same deceleration reads as energy being TRANSFERRED onward to a different body, because the motion stops too abruptly to have simply run out of steam — the source states this distinction explicitly, including naming what ease-out is 'for' (reducing energy) and why this cut deliberately avoids that reading.
purpose: Choose an ease-out's rate deliberately based on where the motion's energy is meant to appear to GO — dissipated in place (slow ease-out) versus handed off to strike something else (fast, snappy ease-out) — rather than treating 'slow down smoothly' as the only correct way to end a fast motion.
visible_effect: A fast head-shake motion comes to a very abrupt, sharp stop rather than gradually decelerating, immediately followed by the energy's effect appearing on a different body (a character being thrown/launched).
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: The source's own direct framing: 'what ease-out is for is reducing the energy — what [the animator] wants to do here is, in a very snappy fashion, transfer all that energy onto a different body, and that's why it's so snappy,' explicitly distinguishing this from a normal ease-out's usual dissipative reading.
physical_interpretation: A genuine physical distinction worth encoding: real momentum transfer between colliding bodies IS abrupt (a fast stop plus a corresponding launch elsewhere), whereas a body slowing under its own friction/air resistance IS gradual — this technique is choosing the ease-out shape to match which real physical scenario is intended, not an arbitrary stylistic pick.
use_cases: a strike or collision where the striking body's motion should read as HANDED OFF to the struck body (a throw, a launch, a knockback) rather than merely stopping
any beat wanting to avoid the 'it just ran out of energy' reading that a standard gradual ease-out implies
non_use_cases: a motion that genuinely IS dissipating in place (coming to rest, no onward transfer to anything else) — a snappy stop there would read as wrong/discontinuous rather than as a handoff, since nothing receives the implied transferred energy

external_force_easing_mismatch's own failure case (LESSONS.md check #10) — an eased-IN key on a declared impact marker is a different, opposite-direction defect (approach softened when it should be sharp); this entry is specifically about the DEPARTURE/ease-OUT side of a beat, and about rate (fast vs. slow) rather than in versus out

style_variations.anime: named directly as a deliberate choice by a specific animator (uton/Tatsuya Yoshihara lineage per the source's surrounding commentary), distinguished explicitly from the 'default' gradual ease-out
style_variations.realistic: the underlying physical logic (abrupt stop = momentum transferred elsewhere, gradual stop = energy dissipated in place) applies directly to realistic motion too, making this one of this batch's more physically-grounded (less purely stylistic) findings

cadence_representation: Directly measurable and directly authorable today: `ai/motion.js sampleMotion`'s velocity curve already reports how quickly a deceleration reaches zero (the ease-out's own rate/shape), and `set_easing`/keyframe interpolation already lets an author choose a snappy versus gradual ease-out curve. What is missing is the SEMANTIC link this entry describes: nothing currently checks an ease-out's rate against whether the same moment declares an onward energy-transfer event (e.g. a linked launch/knockback on another item) versus no such event, the same kind of marker-plus-curve join `external_force_easing_mismatch` (check #10) is built around.
control_surface: `set_easing` already authors the ease-out rate directly; no check currently cross-references it against a declared energy-transfer/impact-recipient event.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Directly buildable with existing measurements: `sampleMotion`'s velocity-to-zero rate on the ending item, cross-referenced against `ai/events.js` markers on a SECOND item (the implied recipient) starting near the same instant — a fast ease-out with no corresponding recipient event would be the interesting edge case to flag, symmetrical to check #10's own marker-plus-curve join.
generation_or_modification_methods: `set_easing` can already author either a gradual or snappy ease-out; nothing currently proposes the choice based on a declared energy-transfer intent.
failure_modes: a gradual ease-out on a strike meant to read as transferring momentum onward, undercutting the handoff and making the strike look like it simply ran out of energy
a snappy, abrupt ease-out with no onward recipient of the implied transferred energy, reading as a discontinuity or a cut motion rather than a deliberate handoff
roblox_considerations: Directly authorable via ordinary `AnimationTrack` easing-style selection (e.g. choosing a steep-vs-shallow custom easing curve) on the striking limb/subject's ending keys, paired with a launch/knockback effect timed to the same instant on the receiving character.
examples: 'he innovates with anticipation here, there's no buildup and release — the cut starts with release and then technically eases out, because the dragon's head is coming to a stop here, but the ease-out is done extremely quickly, extremely snappily, so that he can transfer all that energy, because he does not want to reduce the energy here — that's what ease-out is for, right, it's for reducing the energy — what [he] wants to do here is, in a very snappy fashion, transfer all that energy onto a different body, and that's why it's so snappy' (video @ 21:19–21:50)
